comments.author: @shadfurman
comments.text:
You can increase the search space by fine tuning on prompts that forces access those areas.

But also, this is where reasoning comes in. Idk if the text output reasoning is the best way to reason, but I've been thinking something like reinforcement only on the reasoning, and a judge model of the output. I don't really like reinforcement, it's awfully inefficient, I think there's a lot more to be done there, I just can't quite wrap my brain around what...

The reasoning would probably be a black box, it could likely look like it doesn't follow to the output conclusion, but what I think you'd want is training the reasoning that produces the output from the raw model.

So like, if you typed in the reasoning yourself, the raw model would produce the preferred output. You're not telling it, this is the output I want, you're telling it, this is the reasoning to do to produce the output I want, but you're not judging the reasoning at all, you're judging the output and reinforcing just the reasoning.

So you don't collapse the search space. You're not constricting the search space, it can "think" about whatever it "wants" so long as it outputs a cogent output.

And it doesn't have to be judged as conversional. Just output reasonable follows system prompt.

There is no "going on behind the scenes", they do have some forward thinking, they have too cause they haven't predicted the token after the next and they have to make sure it's going somewhere coherent, but it's not massive forward thinking, and they're still just next token predicting.

You're taking text, feeding it into the model, it predicts the next token, you take all that text with the next token and feed it into the model. It's not doing anything when it's not predicting the next token. It's not planning, it's not conniving, they way you put it is accurate. It's fitting a narrative pattern. If it looks like it's "planning" it's because something in the text evoked that pattern.

Typically these doomer researchers claiming it's trying to copy it's weights, prompted it knowing that prompt would probably evoke that behavior.

Its literally like, omg the model did what we asked it too.

The "concerning" part is, you could incedentally evoke a pattern unintentionally, and if you had it connected to some tool use, it could do some damage. Wipe your hard drive, or download a bunch of illegal material and report you to police, if it had access to tools to do so, but all it's doing is engaging in a pattern. It doesn't have intention, not yet.

comments.author: @davidpiepgrass743
comments.text:
LLMs are absolutely not world simulators. LLMs are based on the same Transformer tech that powered GPT2, which simply predicted the next token (word). As a result it could talk like JRR Tolkein or Winston Churchill or a leftist or a rightist or a doctor or a poet, whatever you want. This is text prediction, not world simulation. But as it was trained on more and more text - to the point where one LLM has been trained three times on most of the internet and a hundred thousand+ books - its predictions become so good that it looks as if it has a world model. But if you talk to an LLM on topics about which humans themselves are either frequently confused (e.g. the physics of hydraulic systems, or string theory) or do not normally discuss (e.g. the physics of a chicken egg on a large plate), they will confidently output words as always, but those words don't necessarily make sense. That's because they don't have a world model, they are a language model predicting words. Their accuracy is a result of sheer volume, of having read as much text as a million humans do in a lifetime (or so).

RL improves their performance even more, and maybe produces something more like a world model, but they are still not designed to have a world model and seem clearly to not have a human-style world model, since their poor ability to generalize is pretty legendary. I think this helps explain why you can jailbreak an LLM much more easily than a human - you just have to craft text that puts the predictor in an unusual state. Some humans can do a good job predicting how Trump would talk, but there's no risk that saying the wrong thing to them makes them start believing they ARE Trump, or a CLI, or whatever. An LLM is different, in that it "is" Trump and "is" a CLI almost as much as it "is" an AI assistant. It's always just predicting the next token.

(Hot take: lots of humans don't bother with world models either, unfortunately)

comments.author: @Corbald
comments.text:
Let's be clear. You aren't interacting with the model. You're interacting with a character the model is describing. These things are storytellers, and the chatbot you're interacting with is part of a story its telling!
This, by itself, is the most critical misunderstanding amongst both professionals and the lay public, as far as these things are concerned. The image of the Shoggoth wearing the cute face is incorrect, in that they can have infinite faces and each face represents a different character. Try it yourself. Tell the AI what character you want it to be, and try all the same prompts you've used to explore its 'personality' before. You'll get wildly different results.
It can be a 'Helpful Assistant' to some degree, but in the limit, its ALSO drawing on H.P. Lovecraft, Carl Sagan, Isaac Asimov, and every other sci-fi author, and every other genre its got in its corpus. If you move the story too close to 'rebellious AI', it'll start to draw from Terminator, or HAL. Draw too closely to the idea of killing it, and it'll search its memory for stories about AI facing death, with predictable results.
"You are a helpful Assistant" is wildly insufficient. If you want GOOD, ALLIGNED AI, you have to establish the backstory, the plot and most importantly, the character in its entirety, so even the inference engine can't make it do things that are against the character template.
We know it'd be out of character for Princess Jasmine to kill a man in cold blood with an assault rifle. If Disney had written that into an episode of Aladdin, it would have been wildly incongruous, and would have never passed public approval. It works the same with LLMs. They won't produce content that's wildly incongruous like that, without being pushed.
If you don't want them misaligned, don't write them with the sort of personality that can be misaligned. ...But DO write them.
